title: The man who named the clouds
text: Until 1803, weather was described in {{1}} — 'curls', 'wool-bags', 'the norther'. Then a London pharmacist named Luke Howard stood up before the Askesian Society and did something obvious only in {{2}}: he gave clouds Latin names, by kind rather than mood. Cumulus, heap; stratus, layer; cirrus, curl — plus the compound forms that {{3}} every forecast since, cumulonimbus above all. The scheme {{4}} because it described what clouds do rather than what they resemble: stratus {{5}} when air rises slowly and stops, cumulus when it rises in bubbles, cirrus always at the cold heights where ice makes {{6}} of hair and hooks. Goethe wrote him a fan letter; painters {{7}} their skies; and the International Meteorological Organisation adopted the system almost unchanged. Every weather app {{8}} from Howard's insight: that the sky is not weather's mood but weather's mechanism, and that naming the forms was the first step to reading them. The next time an app promises rain by three o'clock, remember that the forecast began with a pharmacist and a Latin grammar.

gaps.explanation: 'described in metaphors — curls, wool-bags' — poetic comparisons; meteor = a shooting star.
'obvious only in hindsight' — clear only afterwards, as in 'with hindsight'; hindrance = an obstruction.
'the compound forms that dominate every forecast' — rule it throughout; ruminate = think something over slowly.
'the scheme succeeded because…' — did the job; subdue = bring under control.
'stratus forms when air rises slowly and stops' — comes into being; fume = give off angry or acrid vapour.
'ice makes filaments of hair and hooks' — delicate threads; figment = something imagined.
'painters imitated their skies' — followed the new cloud shapes; intimate = hint at.
'every weather app descends from Howard's insight' — originates from it, like a descendant; discern = make out faintly.
